power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: N ightmares trap people in a unique state of helplessness.
Whereas fear during wake can be resolved with downregulation strategies, fear during sleep typically coincides with a reduction in the cognitive and social routes to implement them.
Here, we report a case in which a dreamer and a technician together overcame both limitations, ending a nightmare in real time.

A participant experiencing frequent nightmares was enrolled in a protocol designed to induce lucid dreams (restoring cognition during REM sleep) and enable communication from the dream via eye movements (restoring a social connection).
During a nightmare, they gained awareness and used the eye signal as a mayday to request extraction from the dream, all while in polysomnography-verified REM sleep.
They were awakened by the technician 34 seconds after the help request and reported immediate relief.
At 2-and 4-week followups, lucid dream frequency increased relative to baseline, with lucidity reducing the distress of a subsequent nightmare.
Together, these results suggest that real-time dream communication might offer an in somno approach to treating nightmares, a core symptom of PTSD and other psychiatric disorders.
Nightmares produce an intense fear with feelings of helplessness 1 .

Unlike waking fear, which can be quelled with social and cognitive emotion regulation, fear during sleep occurs with reduced executive function and behavioral isolation, preventing the deployment of such strategies.
However, lucid dreams are a unique exception 2, 3 and might offer a way to cope with fear during sleep 4.
text.formatted: However, lucid dreams are a unique exception <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">3</ref> and might offer a way to cope with fear during sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">4</ref>.

text.text: Eye movements in a lucid dream are mirrored by physical eye movements and detectable with electrooculography (EOG) 5 .
text.formatted: Eye movements in a lucid dream are mirrored by physical eye movements and detectable with electrooculography (EOG) <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">5</ref> .

text.text: Thus, a common research protocol is to train participants to perform distinct eye-movement patterns before sleep and then use them to timestamp specific moments of the dream from within 6 .
text.formatted: Thus, a common research protocol is to train participants to perform distinct eye-movement patterns before sleep and then use them to timestamp specific moments of the dream from within <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">6</ref> .

text.text: Such EOGbased signaling could provide nightmare sufferers with the ability to send a distress signal from a nightmare and request extraction by a live technician.
Here, we report a case in which a participant in a lucid dream induction study became lucid during a spontaneous nightmare and used a pre-trained eye signal to request extraction from REM sleep.
The participant was awakened in response to the request, reported immediate relief, and described controllable lucid dreams that reduced nightmare distress at follow-ups.
Participant.
The participant (female, age 25-34) was enrolled in a study testing a novel lucid dream induction method 7 .
text.formatted: The participant (female, age 25-34) was enrolled in a study testing a novel lucid dream induction method <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">7</ref> .

text.text: At baseline, they reported dream recall almost every morning, lucid dreams about once a year (with none in the past week), and a mean of 1.1 on the Lucid Dreaming Skills Questionnaire 8 (LUSK;0 = in none to4 = in all lucid dreams).
text.formatted: At baseline, they reported dream recall almost every morning, lucid dreams about once a year (with none in the past week), and a mean of 1.1 on the Lucid Dreaming Skills Questionnaire <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">8</ref> (LUSK;0 = in none to4 = in all lucid dreams).

text.text: On the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index 9 (PSQI), they reported that bad dreams disrupted their sleep once or twice a week.
text.formatted: On the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">9</ref> (PSQI), they reported that bad dreams disrupted their sleep once or twice a week.

text.text: Protocol.
The laboratory night followed the wake-backto-bed (WBTB) protocol of the parent study 7 (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: The laboratory night followed the wake-backto-bed (WBTB) protocol of the parent study <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">7</ref> (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1A</ref>).

text.text: The participant arrived at the laboratory in the evening and was fitted for polysomnography (PSG) with an American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) secondary montage (EEG at Fz, Cz, and Oz; left vertical and right horizontal EOG; chin EMG; respiration).
Before lights out, they were instructed to signal upon becoming lucid by moving their eyes left and right: "Look at your left ear, right ear, left ear, right ear, center" (LRLR) 10 .
text.formatted: Before lights out, they were instructed to signal upon becoming lucid by moving their eyes left and right: "Look at your left ear, right ear, left ear, right ear, center" (LRLR) <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">10</ref> .

text.text: The signal was rehearsed while awake with eyes open and closed until clearly visible on the EOG.
The participant was told that the signal indicated lucidity only, and no instructions were given regarding a distress signal.
However, the standard protocol was to wake the participant within a minute of any LRLR signal to maximize dream recall.
After ∼4 hours in bed, the participant was awakened for ∼40 minutes of behavioral tasks and additional LRLR signal rehearsal, then returned to bed.
A technician monitored PSG in real time throughout the night, scoring sleep visually according to AASM guidelines 11 and watching the EOG channels for LRLR signals.
text.formatted: A technician monitored PSG in real time throughout the night, scoring sleep visually according to AASM guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">11</ref> and watching the EOG channels for LRLR signals.

text.text: Sleep was later staged offline with YASA 12 (v0.8.0).
text.formatted: Sleep was later staged offline with YASA <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">12</ref> (v0.8.0).

text.text: After sleep, a morning interview with open-ended questions about the dream experience was conducted.
The participant completed follow-up surveys 2 and 4 weeks after the laboratory visit, each including a report of a recent dream.
The event of interest occurred during REM sleep ∼2 hours into a morning nap (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: The event of interest occurred during REM sleep ∼2 hours into a morning nap (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1B</ref>).

text.text: At 05:18, the technician observed an LRLR signal on the EOG in REM sleep (as staged both online and offline).
After waiting briefly to confirm it, they woke the participant 34 seconds after signal onset to collect a dream report.
The participant reported that they had been having a nightmare in which "a mob of people . . . pitchforks and torches . . . became very aggressive."
The dream was rated as extremely negative with minimal pleasure and maximal arousal on the Affective Slider 13 .
They "realized . . . this is probably a dream" and immediately attempted "to do the eye thing" more than once.
Likert ratings indicated that they were definitely aware of dreaming and definitely performed the eye signal despite definitely not being able to control the dream.
Critically, the signal the participant had been instructed to use for lucidity was used instead to request emergency extraction, or "a mayday" to say "get me out of here."

Use of the signal while dreaming was later described as analogous to the use of telephones in The Matrix or tapping out in professional wrestling, and also as "a social thing" made possible by knowing that the technician was "there, reachable."
They reported immediate relief upon being awakened, noting they were "having a horrible time" in the dream "but now this is very good."
The technician offered to end the session early, but the participant chose to return to sleep.
Longitudinal follow-ups.
Relative to baseline, lucid dream frequency increased to about once a week at 2 weeks and two to three times a month at 4 weeks.
On the PSQI, bad dreams increased from once or twice a week at baseline to three or more times a week at 2 weeks, then decreased to less than once a week at 4 weeks.

Because the follow-up items asked about the past 2 weeks, whereas the baseline items asked about the past month (PSQI) or gave no time frame (lucid dream frequency), these comparisons are approximate.
A dream reported at 2 weeks was a nightmare that began as "the nightmares I've been having."

Upon becoming lucid during the nightmare, they performed the eye movements again "for good measure," and their rating of the dream shifted from extremely negative before lucidity to somewhat positive after.

They described lucidity as "very helpful," changing the dream "not completely,  During setup, the participant was taught to signal lucidity by looking left-right-left-right (LRLR) and rehearsed the signal awake with eyes open and closed.

(B) The dream report describes a nightmare that turned lucid, the signal sent as a mayday, and relief on awakening (nightmare and lucidity timings are estimated).
In a follow-up, they reported a nightmare at home where they became lucid and again made the eye movements.

but enough to stop it from being anxiety inducing."
The dream reported at 4 weeks was not a nightmare but included lucidity, which shifted the emotional tone from neither positive nor negative to somewhat positive.

Unlike in the laboratory nightmare, they were definitely able to control both dreams, and their lucid dreaming skills in these dreams (LUSK means of 2.3 and 2.0) were higher than at baseline across all their lucid dreams (1.1).

When asked whether the laboratory visit had influenced their subsequent dreams, they pointed to a new sense of agency, noting that "[h]aving agency in such a concrete and grounded way made something switch and make sense in the helplessness I usually feel when having nightmares."
However, they also noted that "the social element of it" was not replicated at home.
Although the reported LRLR signaling was confirmed on visual inspection, we tested whether the signals could be distinguished from other rapid eye movements in sleep.
First, an automated LRLR detector was calibrated on the participant's nine waking rehearsals (size, shape, and speed of their eye movements) and then applied to all 4 hours of sleep.
It identified only two LRLRs, both corresponding to the period immediately before the dream report and consistent with visual inspection (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: It identified only two LRLRs, both corresponding to the period immediately before the dream report and consistent with visual inspection (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1B</ref>).

text.text: Second, to check this without relying on the detector's criteria, every nonoverlapping sequence of four consecutive eye movements in sleep was ranked by its similarity to the rehearsals (Figure 1C).
text.formatted: Second, to check this without relying on the detector's criteria, every nonoverlapping sequence of four consecutive eye movements in sleep was ranked by its similarity to the rehearsals (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1C</ref>).

text.text: The two LRLR signals were ranked first and second of all 85 non-overlapping sequences, and the third rank was a left-right-left-left sequence shortly after.
To our knowledge, this is the first reported case of realtime communication from a nightmare followed by immediate extraction of the dreamer.
Events like this are difficult to capture, as lucid dreams are infrequent for most people 14 and nightmares rarely occur in the laboratory, let alone together.
text.formatted: Events like this are difficult to capture, as lucid dreams are infrequent for most people <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">14</ref> and nightmares rarely occur in the laboratory, let alone together.

text.text: Although the current case comes from a single unplanned event in a non-clinical setting, the combination of live PSG, lucid dream induction, EOG communication, and longitudinal follow-ups makes it an informative example of how dream engineering 15 might be applied in sleep medicine.
text.formatted: Although the current case comes from a single unplanned event in a non-clinical setting, the combination of live PSG, lucid dream induction, EOG communication, and longitudinal follow-ups makes it an informative example of how dream engineering <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">15</ref> might be applied in sleep medicine.

text.text: Could a lucid dreamer just wake themselves up?
Intentional awakening from a lucid dream is one way to resolve nightmares 16 , but levels of lucidity vary widely 17 and lower levels are associated with reduced awakening success 18 .
text.formatted: Intentional awakening from a lucid dream is one way to resolve nightmares <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">16</ref> , but levels of lucidity vary widely <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">17</ref> and lower levels are associated with reduced awakening success <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">18</ref> .

text.text: Importantly, being aware of the dream while unable to change it has the potential to make a nightmare worse by inducing heightened fear relative to a non-lucid nightmare 19 .
text.formatted: Importantly, being aware of the dream while unable to change it has the potential to make a nightmare worse by inducing heightened fear relative to a non-lucid nightmare <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">19</ref> .

text.text: The current participant reported being unable to control the dream and made no attempt to wake up, yet still produced the LRLR signal, suggesting that a deliberate eye signal might remain available even under limited control.
Thus, a technician prepared to wake the dreamer offers a backup when lucidity does not suffice.
The LRLR in this study was intended to signal lucidity, not distress, and was answered only because the protocol was to wake the participant after any signal.
Adding a second, distress-specific eye signal is a potential fix, but the participant doubted they could have managed one.
Instead, protocols might include a single, unambiguous "safe signal" in a separate modality (e.g., facial muscle contractions 2, 3 ).
text.formatted: Instead, protocols might include a single, unambiguous "safe signal" in a separate modality (e.g., facial muscle contractions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">3</ref> ).

text.text: Future work might also automate realtime detection of these signals to reduce technician burden and allow for at-home devices.
Why might a single rescue have lasting benefits?
One concern is that immediate relief resembles avoidance, which reduces fear in the moment but might maintain nightmares over time.
The follow-up data suggest otherwise, as nightmares persisted but with less distress under greater dream control.
Lucidity alone might reduce longitudinal nightmare distress through increased selfefficacy over dream content 20, 21 and improved morning mood 16, 22 .
text.formatted: Lucidity alone might reduce longitudinal nightmare distress through increased selfefficacy over dream content <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">21</ref> and improved morning mood <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">22</ref> .

text.text: In the current case, knowing that someone was reachable in the laboratory reduced the isolation that otherwise accompanies fear during sleep, suggesting the experience of connection also played a positive role.
Current nightmare treatments 23 , such as Image Rehearsal Therapy and Lucid Dreaming Therapy, operate in vigilia.
text.formatted: Current nightmare treatments <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">23</ref> , such as Image Rehearsal Therapy and Lucid Dreaming Therapy, operate in vigilia.

text.text: The patient sets intentions while awake with the goal of changing nightmare content when it recurs, but the dreamer is ultimately alone once the nightmare begins.
In contrast, here and elsewhere 24, 25 , dream engineering 15 increasingly acts in somno to offer external support systems as the nightmare occurs.
text.formatted: In contrast, here and elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">25</ref> , dream engineering <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">15</ref> increasingly acts in somno to offer external support systems as the nightmare occurs.
